Survey of India Map Sheet No. G43S7 and 20 cm of twine supplied; the outline map of India must be detached, marked and fastened to the answer booklet. Q1 (toposheet map reading) is omitted: the school paper was shared without its Survey of India map extract.

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(i) Assertion (A): Tamil Nadu receives most of its rainfall from the North-east Monsoon.
Reason (R): It lies in the rain shadow region of the Western Ghats.

options.a: A is true, but R false.
options.b: A is false, but R is true.
options.c: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.d: Both A and R are true, and R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution: (c) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.. Lying in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats, Tamil Nadu gets little rain from the SW monsoon; hence most of its rain comes from the NE (retreating) monsoon that picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal.

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(ii) The process by which the top layer of soil is removed due to agents like wind and water is called
questions.solution: (b) Soil erosion. Removal of top soil by wind/water is soil erosion.

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(iii) Which type of vegetation is depicted in the image?
questions.solution: (b) Montane Forest. The image shows tall, conical coniferous trees on mountain slopes - typical Himalayan montane forest.
questions.figure_desc: Photograph of conical coniferous trees on mountain slopes

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(iv) "A multipurpose river valley project built on the river Mahanadi is used for irrigation, power generation and flood control." Which project is this?
questions.solution: (b) Hirakud. Hirakud dam is on the Mahanadi in Odisha.

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(v) Ravi's factory uses a mineral that is the chief ore of aluminium. It is extracted in Odisha and Jharkhand. Which mineral is he using?
questions.solution: (a) Bauxite. Bauxite is the chief ore of aluminium.

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(vi) Assertion (A): Tea plantations are found mainly in the hill slopes of Assam and Darjeeling.
Reason (R): Tea requires stagnant water for its growth.

options.a: A is true, but R false.
options.b: A is false, but R is true.
options.c: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.d: Both A and R are true, and R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution: (a) A is true, but R false.. A is true; R is false - stagnant water is harmful to tea roots, which is why tea is grown on well-drained hill slopes.

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(vii) The method of growing crops and rearing livestock on the same farm is called ____ farming.
questions.solution: (c) Mixed. Mixed farming combines crops and livestock.

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(viii) BHEL and SAIL are categorised under which of the following industries?
questions.solution: (a) Public Sector Industries. Both are owned and run by the Government of India.

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(ix) If you need to transport perishable goods over a short distance, which mode of transport will you use and why?

options.a: Air transport because it is the fastest.
options.b: Road transport because it offers door-to-door service.
options.c: Water transport because it handles heavy loads.
options.d: Rail transport because it is economical.

questions.solution: (b) Road transport because it offers door-to-door service.. For short distances road transport is quick, flexible and offers door-to-door delivery.

questions.question:
Choose the correct answers from the given options. (Only write the answers.)
(x) Identify the waste management practice shown in the image:
[Image: four separate bins labelled Wet Waste (green), Dry Waste (blue), Sanitary Waste (red) and E-Waste (black).]
questions.solution: (c) Waste Segregation. Separating waste into different bins at source is waste segregation.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Riya, who lives in Mangalore, experiences frequent rain in June, while her cousin Sanya in Bhopal finds it hot and dry during the same month.
(a) State one reason for the difference in weather between two cities.
(b) What type of rainfall does Mangalore experience in June?
questions.solution: (a) Mangalore lies on the west coast on the windward side of the Western Ghats and receives the Arabian Sea branch of the SW monsoon first (early June), whereas Bhopal is in the interior, far from the sea, where the monsoon arrives later (mid/late June) - so it remains hot and dry. (b) Orographic (relief) rainfall from the south-west monsoon.

marking_points.point: (a) Coastal/windward location gets monsoon early vs interior location

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: State two factors influencing the onset of the South west monsoon over India.
questions.solution: 1. Intense heating of the north-western plains in summer creates a strong low-pressure area that draws moisture-laden winds from the Indian Ocean. 2. Northward shift of the ITCZ and of the westerly jet stream (which moves north of the Himalayas), along with the easterly jet stream over the peninsula, triggers the sudden burst of the monsoon. (Also: high pressure over the southern Indian Ocean / El Nino conditions.)

marking_points.point: Factor 1 (low pressure over NW India / differential heating)

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a reason for each:
(a) Chennai receives rain twice in a year.
(b) The Western Ghats receive heavier rainfall than the Eastern Ghats.
(c) The Himalayas play an important role in India's climate.
questions.solution: (a) Chennai gets some rain from the SW monsoon (Bay of Bengal branch/thunderstorms) in summer and its main rain from the retreating NE monsoon in Oct-Dec, which picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal. (b) The Western Ghats are high and continuous and lie at right angles to the moisture-laden Arabian Sea branch of the SW monsoon, causing heavy orographic rain on the windward side; the Eastern Ghats are low, broken and parallel to the winds. (c) The Himalayas block the cold, dry polar winds from Central Asia in winter and force the SW monsoon winds to rise and shed rain over north India.

marking_points.point: (a) Rain from both SW and retreating NE monsoons
(b) High continuous Ghats perpendicular to winds vs low broken Eastern Ghats
(c) Block cold winds; trap monsoon winds causing rain

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Study the climatic data given below and answer the following questions:
Month: Jan Feb Mar Apr May Jun Jul Aug Sep Oct Nov Dec
Temp (°C): 15.0 17.2 22.5 28.6 32.8 34.1 33.2 31.5 30.0 26.0 20.5 16.8
Rainfall (cm): 2.4 1.8 1.0 0.6 0.3 12.5 24.3 23.7 14.2 2.6 1.2 2.0
(a) Identify the hottest month and state the temperature.
(b) Does this station experience an equable or continental climate? Give one reason.
(c) What is the annual range of temperature of the station?
questions.solution: (a) June, 34.1°C. (b) Continental climate - the annual range of temperature is high (19.1°C) with very hot summers and cool winters, showing the station is far from the moderating influence of the sea. (c) Annual range = 34.1 - 15.0 = 19.1°C.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Mention any two causes of soil erosion in India.
questions.solution: 1. Deforestation - removal of vegetation cover exposes soil to rain and wind. 2. Overgrazing by animals (also heavy torrential rainfall, faulty farming like ploughing up and down slopes, shifting cultivation).

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Mention two ways in which afforestation helps in preventing soil erosion.
questions.solution: 1. Tree roots bind the soil particles together and hold the soil in place. 2. Tree canopy and leaf litter break the force of falling rain and slow down surface runoff and wind speed, increasing infiltration.

marking_points.point: Canopy/litter reduce impact of rain, runoff and wind

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
With reference to the Black soil, answer the following questions:
(a) Name two crops commonly grown in this soil.
(b) Mention one key physical property of Black Soil.
(c) State one reason why Black soil is called "self-ploughing soil."
questions.solution: (a) Cotton and sugarcane (also jowar, wheat, groundnut). (b) It is clayey, fine-textured and has high moisture-retaining capacity (becomes sticky when wet). (c) It swells when wet and shrinks and develops deep cracks when dry; this allows air to penetrate and the soil turns itself over - hence 'self-ploughing'.

marking_points.point: (c) Cracks on drying aerate the soil

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a reason:
(a) Wind is a common agent of soil erosion in arid region.
(b) Laterite soil is not suitable for cultivation.
(c) Alluvial soil is extensively found in the Northern Plains.
questions.solution: (a) Arid regions have little vegetation cover and loose, dry sandy soil, so strong winds easily blow away the top soil. (b) It is highly leached, poor in nitrogen, lime, potash and humus, and is acidic/porous, hardening like brick on exposure - so it is infertile. (c) The Northern Plains were formed by deposition of silt brought by the Himalayan rivers - Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Sameer travels from the Western Ghats to the Thar Desert on a botanical field visit. He notices thick green forests in one region and sparse, thorny bushes in another region.
(a) Identify the two types of natural vegetation observed by Sameer.
(b) State one climatic condition responsible for each type of vegetation.
questions.solution: (a) Tropical evergreen (rain) forests in the Western Ghats; tropical desert (thorn and scrub) vegetation in the Thar Desert. (b) Evergreen: heavy rainfall above 200 cm with high temperature and humidity throughout the year. Desert: very low rainfall (below 50 cm) with high temperature and long dry period.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
With reference to mangrove forests in India:
(a) Name one region where these forests are found.
(b) Give two adaptations that allow mangrove trees to survive in their environment.
questions.solution: (a) The Sundarbans in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta (also Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna deltas, Andaman and Nicobar). (b) 1. Breathing roots (pneumatophores) that grow upward out of the waterlogged, oxygen-poor mud. 2. Stilt/prop roots that anchor the trees in soft mud against tides; leaves tolerate salt water (salt-excreting).

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Give three reasons why forest conservation is needed.
questions.solution: 1. Forests maintain ecological balance and regulate climate, rainfall and the oxygen-carbon dioxide balance. 2. They prevent soil erosion and floods and recharge groundwater. 3. They provide habitat for wildlife (biodiversity) and supply timber, fuel, fodder and raw materials for industries and livelihoods of tribal people.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give a geographical reason for each of the following:
(a) The trees in the Tropical Desert forest have stunted growth.
(b) The Tropical Evergreen Forests are difficult to exploit for commercial purposes.
(c) Forests are grown around the cities having Iron and Steel Industries.
questions.solution: (a) Due to scanty rainfall and very little moisture in the soil, trees cannot grow tall and remain short and stunted. (b) The forests are very dense with undergrowth and creepers, trees of many species grow mixed together (not in pure stands), wood is hard and heavy, and transport facilities are lacking. (c) Trees absorb the smoke, dust and harmful gases emitted by iron and steel plants, reduce air pollution and act as green belts/noise buffers.

marking_points.point: (b) Dense, mixed stands, hard wood, poor transport

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Groundwater levels are depleting rapidly in many parts of India. Explain any two causes for this decline.
questions.solution: 1. Over-extraction through tube wells for irrigation (water-intensive crops like rice and sugarcane) and for urban/industrial use, faster than natural recharge. 2. Reduced recharge - deforestation and concrete/paved urban surfaces prevent rain water from seeping into the ground; erratic rainfall adds to it.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) Mention the ways by which you as an individual can reuse and conserve water.
(b) Define the term - Inundation Canal.
questions.solution: (a) Reuse water used for washing vegetables/RO waste water to water plants or clean floors; turn off taps while brushing, repair leaking taps and harvest rooftop rain water. (b) An inundation canal is a canal taken directly from a river without any barrage/weir, which carries water only during the rainy season when the river is in flood.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Read the case study given below and answer the following questions:
"In the village of Tikari, the panchayat has installed rooftop rainwater harvesting tanks in all homes. The water is stored in underground tanks and used throughout the dry season."
(a) What type of water conservation method is being practised?
(b) Why is this method suitable for semi-arid regions?
(c) State one environmental benefit of this practice.
questions.solution: (a) Rooftop rainwater harvesting. (b) Semi-arid regions receive scanty, seasonal rainfall and have scarce surface water; storing every drop of rain that falls during the short rainy season ensures water supply in the long dry season. (c) It recharges groundwater and raises the water table (also reduces runoff, soil erosion and urban flooding).

marking_points.point: (b) Scanty seasonal rainfall stored for dry season

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Study the picture given below and answer the following questions:
(a) Identify the irrigation method shown in the picture.
(b) Mention any two advantages of this method.
questions.solution: (a) Sprinkler irrigation. (b) 1. Saves water - water is sprayed evenly like rain with little wastage, suitable for water-scarce areas. 2. Can be used on uneven/sloping land and sandy soils without levelling; fertilisers can be applied with the water.
questions.figure_desc: Photograph of rotating sprinklers spraying water over a crop field

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) State the uses of Manganese.
(b) State one advantage of nuclear energy.
questions.solution: (a) Manganese is used in making iron and steel (hardens steel, ferro-manganese alloy), and in making bleaching powder, insecticides, paints and dry-cell batteries. (b) A very small quantity of nuclear fuel (uranium/thorium) produces a huge amount of energy, and it does not emit greenhouse gases.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) Petroleum is versatile in nature. Explain.
(b) Name two major oil fields of India.
questions.solution: (a) Petroleum is used in many ways - as fuel for transport and power (petrol, diesel, kerosene, aviation fuel), as lubricant, and as raw material for petrochemical industries producing plastics, synthetic fibres, fertilisers, dyes and medicines. (b) Mumbai High (Maharashtra offshore) and Digboi (Assam) (also Ankleshwar - Gujarat, Naharkatiya - Assam).

marking_points.point: (a) Varied uses - fuel, lubricant, petrochemical raw material

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) Anthracite is the best variety of Coal. Explain.
(b) Name the major minerals found in Jharkhand.
questions.solution: (a) Anthracite has the highest carbon content (80-95%), least moisture and volatile matter, burns with a smokeless blue flame and gives maximum heat. (b) Coal, iron ore, copper, mica, bauxite and manganese (also uranium at Jaduguda).

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) Mention the uses of using biogas.
(b) Name an area where abundant wind energy is harnessed.
(c) What are the advantages of using solar energy?
questions.solution: (a) Biogas is used as cooking fuel and for lighting in rural areas, and the slurry left behind is used as rich organic manure. (b) Muppandal (Kanyakumari, Tamil Nadu) (also Jaisalmer in Rajasthan, Gujarat coast). (c) Solar energy is renewable and inexhaustible, freely available, non-polluting and can be used in remote areas for cooking, heating and electricity.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Look at the picture given below and answer the questions based on it.
[Picture: women plucking tea leaves on a tea estate, carrying baskets on their backs.]
(a) Define the term fine pluck.
(b) Why are mountain slopes preferred for tea plantation?
questions.solution: (a) Fine plucking is the plucking of only the top two leaves and a bud of the tea shoot, which gives the best quality tea. (b) Tea needs heavy rainfall but water must not stagnate at the roots; hill slopes provide good drainage (and the cool, humid climate suits tea).

marking_points.point: (b) Slopes ensure drainage - no water stagnation

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Differentiate between two major fibre crops of India.
questions.solution: Cotton vs Jute: 1. Cotton is a kharif crop of the Deccan/black soil regions (Gujarat, Maharashtra) needing moderate rainfall (50-100 cm) and a frost-free period with bright sunshine; jute grows in the hot, humid Ganga-Brahmaputra delta (West Bengal, Assam) needing heavy rainfall (150-250 cm) and standing water for retting. 2. Cotton fibre is obtained from the boll (seed hair) and used for textiles; jute fibre is obtained from the stem (bark) and used for gunny bags, carpets and ropes.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) State the importance of agriculture in India.
(b) State any two problems of Indian agriculture.
questions.solution: (a) Agriculture provides food to the huge population and employs about half of the workforce; it supplies raw materials to industries (cotton, jute, sugarcane) and contributes to exports and national income. (b) 1. Small and fragmented landholdings. 2. Dependence on erratic monsoon rains / lack of irrigation, low yields, poor credit and marketing facilities.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give reasons for the following:
(a) Pulses are grown as rotation crops.
(b) Uttar Pradesh is the largest producer of wheat in India.
(c) Sugarcane cultivation is gaining importance in Peninsular India.
questions.solution: (a) Pulses are leguminous; their root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen and restore soil fertility, so they are rotated with other crops. (b) UP has a vast fertile alluvial plain, cool winters, winter rain from western disturbances and an extensive canal and tube-well irrigation network. (c) The tropical climate of the peninsula gives a longer growing season, higher sucrose content and yield per hectare, better irrigation and well-managed cooperative sugar mills (Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu).

marking_points.point: (c) Tropical climate - higher yield/sucrose, longer crushing season, cooperatives

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Name the major by-products of sugar industry and state their uses.
questions.solution: 1. Bagasse - used as fuel in the mills and for making paper, cardboard and fibre board. 2. Molasses - used to make alcohol (ethanol), rum, yeast and cattle feed. (Press mud - used as manure/wax.)

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: Mumbai is the most important cotton textile center in India. Explain.
questions.solution: Humid coastal climate suits spinning; a natural harbour/port to import machinery and long-staple cotton and export cloth; nearness to the cotton-growing black soil areas of Maharashtra and Gujarat; availability of capital, cheap labour, hydel power and a large market.

marking_points.point: Raw material, capital, labour, power, market

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
With reference to the iron and steel plant located at Jamshedpur (Tatanagar), answer the following questions:
(a) From where does the plant get its iron ore?
(b) Which River provides water to the township?
(c) Name the states that provide the labour force.
questions.solution: (a) From Noamundi (Singhbhum district, Jharkhand) and Gurumahisani (Mayurbhanj district, Odisha). (b) The Subarnarekha and Kharkai rivers. (c) Jharkhand, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha (also Chhattisgarh).

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give reason:
(a) Bengaluru is a major IT hub.
(b) Rapid Industrialisation is required in India.
(c) Petrochemical products are replacing traditional raw materials.
questions.solution: (a) Bengaluru has many engineering and research institutes (IISc, IIIT) supplying skilled IT professionals, good infrastructure and connectivity, pleasant climate and government support through software technology parks. (b) To generate employment for the large population, reduce dependence on agriculture, increase national income and exports and achieve self-reliance. (c) Petrochemical products like plastics and synthetic fibres are cheaper, durable, light, available in large quantities and do not depend on agriculture, so they replace wood, glass, metal, cotton and jute.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: State the advantage of North South East West Corridor (NSEW).
questions.solution: 1. The North-South Corridor (Srinagar-Kanyakumari) and East-West Corridor (Silchar-Porbandar) provide fast, high-quality 4/6-lane connectivity across the length and breadth of India. 2. They reduce travel time and transport costs, promote trade, industry and tourism and integrate remote regions with the rest of the country.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: What advantages roadways have over railways?
questions.solution: 1. Roads provide door-to-door service and are flexible in route and timing. 2. Roads are cheaper to build and maintain and can be built in hilly, rugged areas; they are economical for short distances and carry perishables quickly.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) Write the advantage of air transport in India.
(b) Name one city where metro rail service is operational.
(c) Name the Inland Waterway connecting Prayagraj to Haldia.
questions.solution: (a) It is the fastest mode, connects remote/inaccessible areas (hills, NE, islands) and is vital during natural calamities for relief. (b) Delhi (also Kolkata, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai). (c) National Waterway 1 (NW-1) on the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly system.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
Give reason:
(a) Railway gauges should be converted into single gauge. Give reasons.
(b) Transport is called as the lifeline of the economy.
(c) Water transport has not much developed in India.
questions.solution: (a) Different gauges cause delays and costs due to trans-shipment of goods and passengers at break-of-gauge points; a uniform broad gauge (Project Unigauge) ensures faster, seamless movement. (b) Transport moves raw materials to industries and finished goods to markets, links producers and consumers, and promotes trade, employment and national integration. (c) Most rivers are seasonal with fluctuating water levels, have silting, waterfalls/rapids and diversion for irrigation; the coastline is smooth with few natural harbours, and rail/road competition is strong.

marking_points.point: (c) Seasonal rivers, silting, few navigable stretches

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: (a) State two advantages of recycling.
questions.solution: 1. It conserves natural resources and raw materials (e.g. trees saved by recycling paper) and saves energy. 2. It reduces the amount of waste going to landfills and reduces pollution of land, water and air.

marking_points.point: Reduces waste in landfills and pollution

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) Awareness about waste management is necessary. Justify.
(b) State two effects of spoilage of landscape.
questions.solution: (a) Only when people understand the harmful effects of improper waste disposal will they segregate waste at source, practise the 3Rs and avoid littering - the success of waste management depends on public participation. (b) 1. Heaps of garbage make the area ugly and foul-smelling, reducing its aesthetic and tourism value. 2. Dumped waste occupies fertile land, breeds flies, mosquitoes and rats and spreads disease.

marking_points.point: (b) Two effects of spoilage of landscape

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question: How can you as a student, help in the reduction of waste?
questions.solution: 1. Use refillable water bottles, steel tiffin boxes and cloth bags instead of disposable plastic. 2. Use both sides of paper, reuse old notebooks and donate old books, clothes and toys. 3. Segregate dry and wet waste at home and school, avoid food wastage and spread awareness through eco-clubs.

questions.choice_note: any 5 of 9 questions in Part II
questions.question:
(a) What is composting?
(b) Write the advantages of Composting.
questions.solution: (a) Composting is the process in which biodegradable organic waste (kitchen waste, leaves, dung) is decomposed by micro-organisms in a pit/heap to form humus-rich manure (compost). (b) 1. Converts waste into rich organic manure that improves soil fertility and structure, reducing the need for chemical fertilisers. 2. Reduces the volume of waste going to landfills and is cheap and eco-friendly.
